notes:
NO HARDWARE WAS TOUCHED. Nothing in hwsupport/ opens a CAN bus, calls can_compat.open_bus(), or constructs yam.arm.YamArm. The USB/CAN device stayed exclusively with Agent C's live bring-up for the whole of this task. Verification is entirely against hwsupport/mock_arm.py. Importing yam.arm is safe and was checked before doing it: yam/can_compat.py's module-level apply() only rebinds GsUsb.start in Python and does not enumerate USB (GsUsb.scan() lives in reset_adapter()/find_adapter(), neither of which is called at import).

WHAT IT IS: hwsupport.keepalive.Keepalive(arm, rate_hz=100.0, on_fault=None) runs a daemon thread that holds the arm's current pose via command_positions() at 100 Hz, so an enabled motor never sees the silent gap that latches 0xD. 100 Hz and the 0.5s gain ramp both come from the driver, not from taste: yam/arm.py's measured note says 20Hz with 0.3-0.4s gaps latched the gripper and 100Hz with zero-torque frames through the gaps did not, and YamArm.hold()/scripts/hold.py ramp gains over the first half second from the pose the arm is already in so torque starts at zero and nothing lurches.

API: start() / stop(timeout=2.0) / pause() / resume() / paused() contextmanager / raise_if_faulted() / .fault / .is_running / .is_paused / .ticks / .events() / .report() / .lock. Module-level keepalive(arm, **kw) contextmanager runs one for a block and surfaces any fault on exit.

HANDOFF: pause() does not just set a flag -- it sets the flag and then acquires the keepalive's RLock, so it returns only once the in-flight six-joint exchange has finished. That matters because yam.arm._exchange resynchronises on a shared receive queue: two threads commanding at once desynchronises frames and hands somebody a joint angle from a different moment. paused() additionally HOLDS that lock for the duration of the block, so a caller that shares it cannot interleave even if the flag races. resume() re-reads the pose the motion left the arm in and restarts the gain ramp.

RECOVERY POLICY (single pass, deliberately): a MotorCommunicationError, or a MotorFaultError whose message is exactly the 0xD text (matched against yam.dm_motor.ERROR_MESSAGES[COMMUNICATION_LOST] so it cannot drift), buys ONE recover_stale_motors() + clear_errors() + enable() pass. clear_errors() is called even when recover_stale_motors() reported nothing stale, and enable() follows because the driver's own docstring says clearing the error does not re-enable the motor. After that single pass is spent -- or if the pass itself fails, or for ANY other fault word (over-temperature, overcurrent, overload) -- the thread stops, stores the exception, logs it, calls on_fault, and every later pause()/raise_if_faulted() raises KeepaliveFaulted. It never retry-loops into a faulted bus. This matches hw_backend.preflight_checklist()'s 'one recovery pass only' line and yam.arm.recover_stale_motors()'s doctrine of clearing the benign timeout latch and only that one. stop() deliberately does NOT disable the motors or close the bus -- the keepalive does not own the arm's lifecycle, and disabling drops the arm limp.

TESTS (35 checks, 3.5s, real threads and real wall-clock because the thing under test is a cadence): [1] the mock's latch has teeth -- a 0.4s silence with no keepalive really does latch every motor; [2] 1.2s beat gap with the keepalive running -> max silence 13ms, zero latches, 102 ticks, held pose unchanged, gains ramped 0.01 -> 0.5; [3] pause/resume around a 0.5s scripted motion -> every exchange inside the window came from the motion's thread and none from the keepalive's, streaming resumed after, pose re-read, no latch across the handoff; [4] injected comms fault -> exactly one recovery -> second fault surfaces instead of retrying, recover_calls stays 1, KeepaliveFaulted raised by raise_if_faulted() and by pause(); [5] a 0xD latch arriving as MotorFaultError also gets the one pass; [6] an overload gets zero recovery attempts and zero clear_errors, surfaced immediately; [7] clean stop -- thread joins, no disable/close, log ends with 'stop', idempotent, refuses to restart in place.

MUTATION-CHECKED, so the suite is not decorative: removing the single-pass guard fails check [4] ('the second comms error stops the thread instead of retrying'), dropping the cadence to 2 Hz fails check [2] ('the thread survived the gap'), and making pause() a no-op fails check [3]. All three mutants exit 1.

MOCK: hwsupport/mock_arm.py reuses the driver's real JointConfig, SafetyLimits, ArmState, MotorFeedback and error codes and defaults to ARM_JOINTS + GRIPPER_JOINT, so a signature drift in yam/ breaks these tests rather than the demo. It models the measured latch (an ENABLED motor silent for > latch_gap_s, default 0.35s, latches 0xD; the latch survives enable and only clear_errors() clears it) and records every exchange with its originating thread name, which is what makes the no-interleave assertion checkable. Fault injection: inject_comms_fault(count) for a silent motor, inject_motor_fault(code) for a physical error word.

FOR AGENT C: arm/hw_backend.py's YamBackend already streams at 100 Hz from connect() to shutdown() and is already the sole owner of the bus, so it is NOT currently latching between beats. What this adds on top is (a) the single-pass recovery policy -- today _stream() catches the error, sets self._fault and dies, and nothing ever attempts recover_stale_motors()/clear_errors() mid-demo, so one transient comms blip ends the demo; (b) an explicit pause()/resume() handoff with a real barrier; (c) a printable event log. Wiring is in my final message. Do not run two streamers at once: if Keepalive is adopted inside YamBackend it must REPLACE _start_streaming()/_stream(), not sit alongside it.
